title: Agentic systems: tool loops, state, cost explosion, compounding failure
story:
A single call answers a single question. Work that requires several dependent steps — look something up, decide, act on the result, check whether it worked — cannot be expressed that way, because each step's input depends on the previous step's output.

The loop is the answer, and Yao and colleagues describe the version worth building: generating reasoning traces and task-specific actions in an interleaved manner, so that reasoning helps induce, track and update action plans and handle exceptions, while actions let the model interface with external sources to gather additional information. They report this overcomes prevalent issues of hallucination and error propagation present in reasoning without grounding.

Their characterisation of the two failure modes it combines against is the useful part, because each is a design people actually ship. Reasoning without acting is not grounded in the external world and uses the model's own internal representations, limiting its ability to reactively explore and update its knowledge — it reasons fluently toward a conclusion nothing checked. Acting without reasoning does not reason abstractly about high-level goals or maintain working memory to support acting over long horizons — it takes plausible next steps and forgets what it was doing.

Then the arithmetic, which is the same shape as the fan-out arithmetic from the failure-modes lesson and just as unforgiving. A component nearly always correct is not nearly always correct enough once a result depends on many of its outputs in sequence. Ten steps at ninety-five percent each is about sixty percent end to end; twenty steps is about thirty-six. Nothing in the loop announces this — each individual step looks reasonable, and it is the product that collapses.

What makes it worse than fan-out is that the steps are dependent rather than parallel. A mistake at step three is not one bad answer among many; it becomes the input to step four, which reasons carefully and correctly from a false premise and produces something coherent and wrong. The loop does not detect the error, it elaborates it.

Three costs compound together and all of them are multiplicative in loop length: money, because every step is a call; latency, because the steps are sequential by construction and cannot be parallelised away; and the probability of at least one mistake. Which gives the design instincts — bound the number of iterations rather than trusting a termination condition the model controls, check results against something outside the model where you can, keep the state explicit rather than accumulated in a growing transcript, and make every tool that changes anything idempotent, because a loop that retries is a loop that will do things twice.

problem.name: Multi-step tool loops
problem.shape: A task needs several dependent steps, where each step's input is the previous step's output.
tell: a model decides what to do next based on what it just did
the transcript grows with every iteration
cost per task varies by an order of magnitude
a wrong early step produces a coherent wrong final answer
problem.move: Interleave reasoning with acting so the plan can be tracked and revised, and ground every step you can against something outside the model. Bound the iteration count externally rather than relying on the model to stop, keep state explicit instead of accumulated in a transcript, and make every state-changing tool idempotent.
problem.invariant: Steps are dependent rather than parallel, so cost, latency and the probability of at least one error all compound with loop length rather than adding.
problem.breaks: An early mistake is not detected, it is reasoned upon. The subsequent steps operate correctly on a false premise and produce a coherent, confident, entirely wrong result — so the failure looks like competent work rather than like an error, which is why it survives review.

cost.time: sequential by construction — the steps depend on each other, so no amount of parallelism shortens the chain
cost.space: a growing context carrying the whole history, which costs money on every subsequent call and eventually exceeds what fits
cost.beats: a single call, which cannot gather information it was not given, and a fixed pipeline, which is predictable and cannot adapt when a step returns something unexpected

worked.problem: Why does a loop of reliable steps produce an unreliable system?
worked.reasoning:
Because the reliabilities multiply rather than average, and because the failures are not independent — an error early becomes a premise later.

The arithmetic first, since it is the part that can be stated exactly. If each step succeeds with probability p and the task needs n dependent steps, end-to-end success is p to the n. At ninety-five percent per step, ten steps is about sixty percent and twenty steps is about thirty-six. Each individual step looks entirely reasonable in isolation; the product is what collapses. This is the same shape as the fan-out arithmetic, where a component that is nearly always fast is not nearly always fast enough once a request depends on many of them.

But dependence makes it worse than that calculation suggests. In a fan-out, a bad response is one bad response among many and can often be discarded. In a loop, the output of step three is the input to step four. So a mistake is not an outlier to be filtered — it is a premise. Step four then reasons carefully and correctly from something false, and produces a coherent result. The loop does not detect the error; it elaborates it. That is why the failure looks like competent work and survives review, and why the end state can be confidently wrong in a way a single bad call rarely is.

The two degenerate designs are worth naming because people ship both. Reasoning without acting is not grounded in the external world and uses the model's own internal representations, which limits its ability to reactively explore and update its knowledge — fluent reasoning toward a conclusion nothing checked. Acting without reasoning does not reason abstractly about high-level goals or maintain working memory over long horizons — plausible next steps with no memory of the objective. The interleaved form exists to combine against both.

So the mitigations, which are mostly about not trusting the loop with things the loop is bad at. Bound the iteration count externally, because a termination condition the model controls is a termination condition that can fail to fire — and an unbounded loop is an unbounded bill. Ground each step against something outside the model wherever possible, since that is what converts a guess into a check. Keep state explicit rather than letting it accumulate in a transcript, because a growing context costs money on every subsequent call and eventually stops fitting. And make every tool that changes anything idempotent, since a loop that retries will do things twice, which is the retries lesson arriving as a hard requirement.

The cost point I would raise unprompted: all three costs are multiplicative in loop length — money, latency and error probability — and the latency is not reducible by parallelism, because the steps are dependent by construction. A system that is affordable at three steps can be unaffordable at fifteen without anything having changed except how hard the task was.

problem.practice: Take an agent you have built and count the steps in a typical successful run. Multiply your per-step success estimate to that power and compare it to your observed success rate. Then find the tool that changes something and check what happens if it is called twice.

beats.broke: A single call answers a single question, and work that requires several dependent steps — look something up, decide, act, check — cannot be expressed as one call.
beats.fix: Put the model in a loop with tools, so it chooses an action, observes a result, and decides again, with reasoning interleaved so the plan can be tracked and revised.
beats.cost: Every step multiplies rather than adds — cost, latency and the probability of a mistake all compound with loop length, and a mistake early is reasoned upon rather than detected.

interview.q: Why does a loop of reliable steps produce an unreliable system?
interview.trap: Stopping at the multiplication. Dependence makes it worse than the arithmetic suggests: an early error is not an outlier to discard but a premise the later steps reason correctly from, producing coherent work that looks competent.
